Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.
Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.
All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

items.title: Valve's patch note supremacy
items.author: Morgan Park
items.summary: To most, the highlight of this week's big Deadlock patch is the snazzy map makeover, new heroes, and tons of quality-of-life additions. To me, it's all about
items.text:
To most, the highlight of this week's big Deadlock patch is the snazzy map makeover, new heroes, and tons of quality-of-life additions. To me, it's all about the patch notes.

I spend a lot of waking hours reading white-text-on-black-background changelogs in this line of work, so when a page comes along that was specifically designed to be pleasant and exciting, it deserves to be rewarded. Valve has a long history of designing beautiful, bespoke webpages to introduce meaningful changes to its games, but the graphics department is really going ballistic with Deadlock.

ValveValveValveValve

(Image credit: Valve)

(Image credit: Valve)The City Never Sleeps patch notes are styled like a tourism brochure for Deadlock's refreshed New York City, walking readers through scenic stops across the four major districts (Chinatown, Theater, Haunted Lot, and Plaza). Descriptions weave between in-world storytelling and technical explanation where it makes sense, with Valve's splashes of humor reminding readers not to take any of this too seriously.

(Image credit: Valve)Dotted lines draw the reader to new points of interest as they scroll while furthering the map motif, and the page is stuffed with custom artwork for new items and mechanics that might only exist there. Valve did such an annoyingly good job with presenting the next era of Deadlock that I'm almost tempted to play a MOBA (but only almost).

Finally, some good food. Welcome back, Valve patch notes.

Valve's golden age of patch notes

September 30, 2010: The Mann-conomy Update (Image credit: Valve)It cannot be understated that Valve pioneered storytelling in multiplayer shooters with Team Fortress 2, arguably kicking off with the 2009 WAR! Update, aka "Soldier vs. Demo." This was before the concept of multiplayer games having seasons, before League of Legends had a TV show, before "live service" was even a thing—Valve had created a cast of nine lovable weirdos and new updates that weren't just dropping items, but telling stories that put the characters in conflict with one another and added context to the multiplayer maps we'd already been fighting in for two years.

It was weird in the first place for an FPS to receive so many free post-launch additions, and it was even weirder for a developer to treat the arrival of new weapons, modes, and hats as worthy of dedicated splash pages with accompanying comic books.

TF2 was the gold standard for post-launch support, and its patch notes drew massive interest, often dropping late on a Thursday or Friday, Pacific time, hinting that Valve may have been polishing until the last minute. Valve's blog posts were never the same month-to-month, often adopting new color schemes, layouts, and original elements for the occasion.

February 24, 2009: The Scout Update (Image credit: Valve)July 8, 2010: The Engineer UpdateValveJune 27, 2012: PyromaniaValveFebruary 24, 2009: The Scout UpdateValveDecember 17, 2009: WAR! UpdateValveThere was no single template they stuck to. The Engineer update introduced his advanced Gunslinger gauntlet and Wrangler as blueprints with hand-written notes, while Scout's update debuted the Force-A-Nature scattergun in a department store catalog. I especially love announcing the Mac version of TF2 with a white, sanitized home page complete with symmetrical boxes and tiny text in the style of Apple circa 2002.

June 10, 2010: The Mac Update (Image credit: Valve)Poring over the "history" section of the TF2 website in 2026 is like uncovering one of those lost civilizations that invented a ton of sophisticated things before everyone else.

April 14, 2011: The Hatless Update (Image credit: Valve)We're in an era marked by formulaic seasons, videogames as advertisement platforms, and teams scrambling to alter plans when they're not immediately popular. And yet 15 years ago, Valve had so much confidence in its direction that it could decide to wage a war between Soldier and Demoman one day (live-tracking the kills between both classes—Soldier narrowly won with 6.40M kills to the collective Demomen's 6.37M), introduce a crafting system the next, and then rebrand as Scream Fortress for October.

It wasn't exclusively good vibes—Valve caught flak for its (now quaint) paid hats, paid loot boxes, and speculative marketplace that became a fixture of updates. In a move that I would be surprised to see a studio make today, Valve made fun of itself at the time with a subsequent "Hatless Update".

Deadlock's blogs are practically retro, it feels weird to say. I wonder what inspired Valve to go this hard again. Counter-Strike 2 and Dota 2's changelogs do not share the same sense of theater. Their patch notes are comparatively regular, functional bullet lists—perhaps in line with how often those games are updated. Valve does occasionally produce unique web pages for major CS2 announcements or Dota 2 events, but we're far from the days when an incremental Mann VS Machine update was announced with a lavish movie poster in the style of kaiju cinema.

December 20, 2012: The Mecha Update (Image credit: Valve)TF2's exceptional, ever-changing patch notes were a reflection of the game they promoted. Valve leveraged the flexibility of an arena shooter and imagined a world where Red and Blu were real factions locked in stupid conflicts. You never really knew what elaborate scenarios Valve would think up next for its over-the-top action figures, and that filled TF2 fans with a sense of wonder that very few games have pulled off since. Maybe it's no coincidence that the only example of innovative multiplayer storytelling in recent years, Helldivers 2, is another over-the-top war game that finds comedy in the futility of endless violence.

Valve is tapping into that dormant TF2 energy in small ways with Deadlock, and it's great, though I wonder if, being a MOBA, the game's inherent sweat level will eventually lead to a regimented, low-nonsense future that's more focused on the minutiae of balance. Whatever Deadlock is up to years from now, I'll be keeping up with the patch notes.

items.title: For once, I'm happy to see expensive corporate lawyers forcing a fan project offline
items.author: andy.chalk@pcgamer.com (Andy Chalk)
items.summary: I don't typically have much love for billion-dollar corporations dropping the 'meet our legal department' hammer on no-budget modders who are just trying to
items.text:
I don't typically have much love for billion-dollar corporations dropping the 'meet our legal department' hammer on no-budget modders who are just trying to exercise their creative muscles, but in this one instance I'm willing to let it slide: Bethesda has issued a cease-and-desist order to an "AI creator" who made a Fallout game set in New York City that runs in browsers.

That's actually overstating it: As Chris First explained in his X feed (via RPS), he "directed Claude and a studio of AI agents" to make the game for him. Nor was there any new creative thought injected into the process, First continued, saying he asked for a game that was "not inspired by" Fallout, but that was "exactly like Fallout."

This is the result.

Fallout: New York, a full Fallout game you play in your browser, built with Claude Opus 5.5.Quests. Dialogue trees. V.A.T.S. A working Pip-Boy.Zero texture files. Zero sound files. Every building, weapon, face and sound is generated by code. pic.twitter.com/58Vls0mOYxSeptember 28, 2026

I know that being playable in a browser is a limiting factor, but this is really just something I'd rather not play at all. It stands in such sharp contrast to mods like Fallout: London or Skyblivion, efforts that reflect genuine passion, commitment, and creativity—and yes, those mods are massive undertakings that require years of effort from hundreds of volunteers, but they also don't suck and I feel like maybe there's a lesson to be learned there.

Anyway, whether I want to play it or not is now a moot point, because yesterday First said he received a message from ZeniMax Media telling him to knock it off—specifically, that the domain name he registered for the project, fallout.nyc, infringes on the studio's IP rights.

(Image credit: Chris First (Twitter))I don't know if First was expecting sympathy for his plight, but he doesn't seem to be getting much of it. Some responses criticize him for calling the project "Fallout," which is just about daring Bethesda to do something, but there's also plenty of heat over the use of AI to make the thing. A few optimists suggest First would be fine if he just changed the name, but he doesn't seem inclined to pursue that course.

That's probably for the best: Maybe I'm being overly harsh here (although I don't think so) but the one clear drawback to that plan is that changing the name doesn't change the fact that it looks like garbola. Playing a low-poly Fallout in a browser isn't an especially impressive technical feat—you can do the same with Morrowind, and it actually looks like Morrowind—and if you just want some really cheap Fallout, Fallout 3 is $2.49 in the Steam Autumn Sale, or you can snag New Vegas for a fiver.

I do sympathize with First's urge for a proper new Fallout game: I'm a little tired of the formula, but it's been 11 years since Fallout 4 and that's too damn long. But this ain't it, as the kids say, and while I'm never going to sign up for the corporate cheerleading squad, I can't say I'm sorry to see this one consigned to the dustbin, where it belongs.

items.title: Possible Love is an excellent layoff movie, and an alarming recession indicator
items.author: Monica Castillo
items.summary: Lee Chang-dong’s layered drama Possible Love, running the festival circuit before hitting Netflix in November, is a movie for now. Following the intricate
items.text:
Lee Chang-dong’s layered drama Possible Love, running the festival circuit before hitting Netflix in November, is a movie for now. Following the intricate pains and desires of two couples whose lives intersect for the shooting of a documentary, the Burning filmmaker’s new movie is about rising economic unease, class divisions, and how it all affects people. It’s also one of the most poignant recent depictions of the grief that comes from losing one’s job, and the fallout that comes with it—all of which, sadly, feels all too relatable for many around the world.


Lee follows Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who was laid off from his longtime employer, and his wife Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon). As she steps up to help the family in a new factory, they meet documentarian Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her entrepreneur husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), who want to feature the couple’s story in Ye-ji’s latest project about layoffs from corporate restructuring. Their lives become intertwined as first Mi-ok then Ho-seok share their experiences of his lob loss. They become so entangled in each other’s lives, in fact, that the line between documentarian and subject starts to blur.


﻿﻿


More than just a plot point for Possible Love, the grief Ho-seok and Mi-ok share is carefully presented and deeply felt. Mi-ok is more forthcoming about her emotions and memories, sharing her experience of solidarity and support in the wake of the layoffs among fellow laid-off employees, as well as the social excommunication she felt after her husband’s job was cut. She explains their life changes in both major and less noticeable ways: Not only did she have to get a job at a different factory while her husband looked for work, but Ho-seok’s carefully carved marble table outside their home never got to welcome any parties after he lost the means to host gatherings.


Through conversations for the film-within-the-film, the couple unpack their pain, shame, guilt, and sometimes overwhelming grief that can only be greeted with tears over the loss of identity, purpose, and means to provide for their families, including the couple’s young son. In one of Possible Love‘s most tense moments, the distant father follows one of his still-employed ex-colleagues who’s buying a birthday cake for their child, the same he was doing for his son. But he follows them further, going to the restaurant where they’re celebrating with a hearty meal and, eventually, the nice cake. He-seok sulks in the shadow of his former life, a ghost only another waiter seems to notice. In group therapy sessions, other workers share similar experiences lamenting their former lives. They felt like they were treated like the walking dead, compared to their still-employed counterparts they considered “the living.” Through no fault of their own, they not only lost their livelihood, they lost something representative of life.


Although America may not officially be in a recession, that hasn’t eased the overall economic fears of many after so many have been affected by the waves of recent layoffs because of corporate restructuring, mergers and acquisitions, and the fears around whatever the looming threat of AI will do to the workforce. South Korea, like the United States, has also weathered a number of high-profile layoffs, including the devastating round that inspired Lee to start working on the script for Possible Love. At a Q&A at the New York Film Festival, Lee said he developed the character of the documentarian in order to explore their experiences, because even he was unsure if he would be the right one to tell that kind of story.


﻿


This isn’t the first time a crummy economy, job insecurity, and rampant unemployment has made its way into the pictures. Back in the days of the Great Depression, comedies like Sullivan’s Travels, It Happened One Night, and My Man Godfrey touched on the issues of the time, acknowledging the hardships many in the audience were experiencing, but with a glamorous sense of escapism. Even the Mervyn LeRoy/Busby Berkeley musical Gold Diggers Of 1933 can’t escape the realistic struggle of its tenuously employed chorus girls, whose shows are closed by the bank faster than they can open to audiences. A drama like Frank Borzage’s Man’s Castle dove deeper into the insecurity shouldered by Spencer Tracy’s character as he tries to help a fellow unemployed love interest, but he’s afraid of married family life because he can’t guarantee that he can afford it.


Another wave of layoff movies welled up after the 2008 financial crisis. Downsizing became the enemy of the people in movies like Up In The Air and The Company Men. Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Tokyo Sonata followed a laid-off worker so riddled with shame, he hid his firing from his family and proceeded to continue commuting to keep up appearances. While today’s financial pressures have not sunk as deeply as those in the late aughts, Possible Love is the second major Korean release in recent years to take on the topic. Last year, Park Chan-wook’s dark comedy No Other Choice, took a satirical look at a desperate character, Man-su (Lee Byung-hun), who loses his job after 25 years of service. While his family makes do without certain luxuries, and weighs the possibility of losing their home, Man-su takes matters into his own hands, literally eliminating the competition for a shot at the next job that comes up.


While unemployment and layoffs are sometimes the starting dramatic premise or a mere punchline in some movies, Possible Love arrives at the story already in progress. What stands out is not just the act of losing one’s job, but the emotional toll that comes after. Informed by Lee’s interviews with people who have experienced layoffs, it’s a movie that takes its time to sit with these characters and gives them space to process their feelings, perhaps for the first time. The couple’s pent-up feelings of betrayal and abandonment eventually break out, especially as the interviews probe further, acknowledging the depth with which these corporate decisions have real-life lasting effects. Possible Love is a reminder to listen to these stories and sit with those in pain and grief, because the experience of losing one’s work, identity, and community all at once can be crushingly isolating and so much more complicated than a separation agreement.

Informed by Lee’s interviews with people who have experienced layoffs, it’s a movie that takes its time to sit with these characters and gives them space to process their feelings, perhaps for the first time. The couple’s pent-up feelings of betrayal and abandonment eventually break out, especially as the interviews probe further, acknowledging the depth with which these corporate decisions have real-life lasting effects. Possible Love is a reminder to listen to these stories and sit with those in pain and grief, because the experience of losing one’s work, identity, and community all at once can be crushingly isolating and so much more complicated than a separation agreement.

items.title: New Japanese Learning Resources: Winter 2022
items.summary: The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese
items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

items.title: Mental Models That Change How You Think | Bill Gurley
items.author: Vicky
items.summary: Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the
items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
items.author: Holyn Thigpen

items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the lesbian bar mask mandate implosion.

When did we stop throwing dinner parties? According to some recent polls surfaced by The Atlantic, rates have been declining for years. The larger context, with which you may already be familiar, is the loneliness epidemic; the slow tightening of our social circles, the dissolving of our web of relationships both casual and intimate. Fewer gatherings like dinner parties offer less opportunities to nurture these relationships. Fewer close relationships make corralling friends for a dinner party all the more difficult.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. As I reported a couple years ago, some Gen Z’ers are throwing friend-making dinner parties in their own homes. Be the change you want to see in the world. Bake a cake and invite your friends over to eat it with you!

Also in today’s Open Tab: DoorDash unveils new programming, we dip a toe into the $60 rye discourse, more restaurant critics bring back stars, and the psychiatrists prescribing GLP-1s for mental health.

DoorDash Leans in to the AI Rat Race

Last week delivery platform DoorDash paid out an historic $131.5 million settlement to New York City delivery workers. This week it debuted a new text-based AI platform through which you can order groceries and restaurant delivery. The platform builds on the recent uptick of other text-based AI-agents like Instinct and Meta’s Muse. You can sign up for the waiting list to test it in beta, but when I reached out to DoorDash to ask how many people were on the waiting list, all a spokesperson would tell me is that the company is “excited by the early interest we’re seeing.”

Also notable: DoorDash announced a pilot program for autonomous delivery drones in Northern California, partnering with restaurants like Chipotle and Popeyes. Will this program expand to eventually take the jobs of human delivery workers? According to a spokesperson, these drones will be used for a “specific use case—mid-range, time-sensitive, small payload,” and “drones are adding capacity for a specific slice of orders, not pulling volume away from Dashers.”

As the tech evolves, though, it’s hard to imagine the company won’t favor drones and robots to which they will never have to worry about paying out a settlement of more than a hundred million dollars over wage issues.

I ate the $60 loaf of rye so you don’t have to

Much has been made of the new bakery, Rye, by Martin Auer, which opened in New York City’s SoHo almost exactly three weeks ago. It serves just one item: a 3-pound loaf of rye bread made with imported Austrian rye flour. (And, okay, a number of tartines.) The hullabaloo is around the price: $60 per loaf in New York, compared to the mere 14 Euros around Austria, where Auer runs a chain of these bakeries.

Auer has received a decent amount of blowback online. Even grocery chain Lidl clowned the shop publicly. Does Auer deserve the hate? I mean, if you don’t want to buy the bread, just don’t buy the bread, right?

For what it’s worth, when I went to the bakery to talk to Martin’s son Tim, with whom he runs the bakery, he told me the bread is priced to cover the cost of importing the flour, the labor, the size of the loaf—three pounds!—and, notably, the monthly rent on a space in SoHo which, if comparable store fronts are any measure, would likely measure into the several tens of thousands.

The younger Auer also told me the bakery is selling out often, though he wouldn’t specify how many loaves per day are made; he opaquely suggested somewhere between 50 and 300.

Was the bread good? Yeah, it was fine. Kind of dense, nutty, and overall pretty mild in flavor. Was it worth sixty American dollars? To me, it seems steep for any loaf of bread, but as we talked about last week, everything is a luxury item now. It’s all priced accordingly.

The new (old) rules for restaurant critics

Decades ago, we had a clear picture of who restaurant critics were. Among them, Mimi Sheraton, who donned wigs and other disguises to go unrecognized when reviewing. Jonathan Gold expanded readers’ minds by unearthing small hidden gems serving thrilling food. Sometimes they were Anton Ego, probably the most widely known (though fictitious) food critic from Disney’s Ratatouille, who seemed to love writing cruel reviews solely for sport.

In the last few years, newspaper restaurant critics have been rewriting the rules of the game. Though New York magazine’s former critic, Adam Platt, famously dropped anonymity way back in 2013, the first newspaper critic to unmask themself was Alison Cook of the Houston Chronicle in 2012; even Gold unmasked himself in 2015. The major reveals remained quiet for some time, and then since 2019, critics like Soleil Ho (San Francisco Chronicle), Lyndsay C. Green (Detroit Free Press), and Louisa Kung Liu Chu (Chicago Tribune) dropped the performance of anonymity upon taking on the mantle at their respective publications. Only last year, critics at the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, and The Washington Post followed suit.

This is all to say that restaurant criticism is always adapting with the times.

One such policy, the starred review, has been a subject of debate for many papers still publishing restaurant reviews. During the 2020 COVID pandemic, many legacy newspapers paused or retired their starred reviews out of respect for the restaurants and their workers suffering from debilitatingly slow business during the lockdown. Fast-forward to today as publications bring back those same starred ratings. In an era dominated by food and restaurant influencers, the argument the critics (and their editors) make is that star ratings help to give a definitive delineation to restaurant reviews written by true experts in the field.

Hilary, a 39-year-old in California, has had depression for about as long as she can remember, which means she’s tried a lot of antidepressants. Mostly, though, the meds left her unimpressed. Then she began taking a GLP-1. A few months in, she felt like her entire outlook had become more positive.

Hilary’s case isn’t wholly unique. Growing evidence shows that GLP-1s may relieve some symptoms of depression. That’s led psychiatrists to use it as a tool in conjunction with nutritional therapy on their patients. Read on to see how GLP-1s have made it to the therapy couch.

blocks.x: Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the lesbian bar mask mandate implosion.

When did we stop throwing dinner parties? According to some recent polls surfaced by The Atlantic, rates have been declining for years. The larger context, with which you may already be familiar, is the loneliness epidemic; the slow tightening of our social circles, the dissolving of our web of relationships both casual and intimate. Fewer gatherings like dinner parties offer less opportunities to nurture these relationships. Fewer close relationships make corralling friends for a dinner party all the more difficult.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. As I reported a couple years ago, some Gen Z’ers are throwing friend-making dinner parties in their own homes. Be the change you want to see in the world. Bake a cake and invite your friends over to eat it with you!

Also in today’s Open Tab: DoorDash unveils new programming, we dip a toe into the $60 rye discourse, more restaurant critics bring back stars, and the psychiatrists prescribing GLP-1s for mental health.
DoorDash Leans in to the AI Rat Race

Last week delivery platform DoorDash paid out an historic $131.5 million settlement to New York City delivery workers. This week it debuted a new text-based AI platform through which you can order groceries and restaurant delivery. The platform builds on the recent uptick of other text-based AI-agents like Instinct and Meta’s Muse. You can sign up for the waiting list to test it in beta, but when I reached out to DoorDash to ask how many people were on the waiting list, all a spokesperson would tell me is that the company is “excited by the early interest we’re seeing.”

Also notable: DoorDash announced a pilot program for autonomous delivery drones in Northern California, partnering with restaurants like Chipotle and Popeyes. Will this program expand to eventually take the jobs of human delivery workers? According to a spokesperson, these drones will be used for a “specific use case—mid-range, time-sensitive, small payload,” and “drones are adding capacity for a specific slice of orders, not pulling volume away from Dashers.”

As the tech evolves, though, it’s hard to imagine the company won’t favor drones and robots to which they will never have to worry about paying out a settlement of more than a hundred million dollars over wage issues.
I ate the $60 loaf of rye so you don’t have to

Much has been made of the new bakery, Rye, by Martin Auer, which opened in New York City’s SoHo almost exactly three weeks ago. It serves just one item: a 3-pound loaf of rye bread made with imported Austrian rye flour. (And, okay, a number of tartines.) The hullabaloo is around the price: $60 per loaf in New York, compared to the mere 14 Euros around Austria, where Auer runs a chain of these bakeries.

Auer has received a decent amount of blowback online. Even grocery chain Lidl clowned the shop publicly. Does Auer deserve the hate? I mean, if you don’t want to buy the bread, just don’t buy the bread, right?

For what it’s worth, when I went to the bakery to talk to Martin’s son Tim, with whom he runs the bakery, he told me the bread is priced to cover the cost of importing the flour, the labor, the size of the loaf—three pounds!—and, notably, the monthly rent on a space in SoHo which, if comparable store fronts are any measure, would likely measure into the several tens of thousands.
The younger Auer also told me the bakery is selling out often, though he wouldn’t specify how many loaves per day are made; he opaquely suggested somewhere between 50 and 300.

Was the bread good? Yeah, it was fine. Kind of dense, nutty, and overall pretty mild in flavor. Was it worth sixty American dollars? To me, it seems steep for any loaf of bread, but as we talked about last week, everything is a luxury item now. It’s all priced accordingly.
The new (old) rules for restaurant critics

Decades ago, we had a clear picture of who restaurant critics were. Among them, Mimi Sheraton, who donned wigs and other disguises to go unrecognized when reviewing. Jonathan Gold expanded readers’ minds by unearthing small hidden gems serving thrilling food. Sometimes they were Anton Ego, probably the most widely known (though fictitious) food critic from Disney’s Ratatouille, who seemed to love writing cruel reviews solely for sport.

In the last few years, newspaper restaurant critics have been rewriting the rules of the game. Though New York magazine’s former critic, Adam Platt, famously dropped anonymity way back in 2013, the first newspaper critic to unmask themself was Alison Cook of the Houston Chronicle in 2012; even Gold unmasked himself in 2015. The major reveals remained quiet for some time, and then since 2019, critics like Soleil Ho (San Francisco Chronicle), Lyndsay C. Green (Detroit Free Press), and Louisa Kung Liu Chu (Chicago Tribune) dropped the performance of anonymity upon taking on the mantle at their respective publications. Only last year, critics at the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, and The Washington Post followed suit.
This is all to say that restaurant criticism is always adapting with the times.

items.title: A Tasting Room With One of NYC’s Largest Wine Lists Debuts in Flatiron
items.summary:
The scallop dish at Amphora. | Alex Staniloff

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in September 2026.
items.text:
The scallop dish at Amphora. | Alex Staniloff

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in September 2026. Throughout the month, we’ll update the list weekly (see: August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January). When we’ve been to a place, we will then include a few openings on our heatmaps (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, cocktail bars) to let you know the ones we like. If there’s an opening in your neighborhood that we’ve missed, let us know at ny@eater.com.

September 9

Spotlight

Flatiron: Amphora, a tasting room boasting one of the city’s biggest wine collections, opens on Wednesday, September 9, in the long-closed home of oenophile favorite Veritas. Executive chef Jack Logue (formerly of now-closed the Lambs Club and Betony) sends out three- and four-course menus, with a la carte options at the bar. Named for the ancient vessel used to transport wine across civilizations, Amphora is stocked with over 2,500 labels — making it one of NYC’s largest wine cellars. Wine director Chris Miller, a fellow Lambs Club alum, spotlights regions like Burgundy, Northern Rhone, Piedmont, and Champagne from top producers that include Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Coche-Dury, Raveneau, and Rousseau. 43 E. 20th Street, at Rutherford Place

And the rest…

Bed-Stuy: Mexican restaurant Olmo doubles down on the block with a collaborative new all-day taqueria and cafe called Peral. The team-up with Mexico City cafe and bar Cicatriz opened right next door to Olmo on Wednesday, September 2. Peral’s menu leans more casual than Olmo (see: tacos, many of which are guisados) with an affinity towards vegetarian and vegan options. 105 Saratoga Avenue, near Decatur Street

Chelsea: Vegan cinnamon roll bar Cinnaholic opened its first physical location in Chelsea over Labor Day weekend, inviting customers to jazz up gooey rolls with customizable toppings like fresh fruit, cookie dough, and chocolate drizzle. Coffee Project New York supplies the caffeine on-site. 228 Eighth Avenue, at West 22nd Street

Crown Heights: Brooklyn’s acclaimed Haitian patty pop-up Bon Pâtés debuted its first physical storefront over Labor Day weekend. Walk-up hours for its freshly baked patties are Thursday to Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., and catering and nationwide shipping are also still available. 637 Nostrand Avenue, at St Marks Avenue

Greenpoint: The owners of Wasabi, the Brooklyn sushi staple that closed this summer after a 26-year run, are back in the game with a new Japanese spot down the street. Ayune, which opened on Monday, September 7, specializes in hand rolls filled with the likes of tuna, salmon, shiitake mushrooms, or Japanese pumpkin, available in sets of three, four, five, or six ($19 to $38). Ayune takes over the former home of Botbar — a robot-run cafe with vegan food from Wasabi. At Ayune, expect a pared-down selection of Wasabi’s familiar favorites, owners Robby and Cristin Wijaya tell Greenpointers. While a beer and wine license awaits, Ayune serves nonalcoholic options like spicy mango coolers, yuzu shiso fizzes, lemonade, and teas. 664 Manhattan Avenue, between Norman and Nassau avenues

Long Island City: At Rewind — a 9,000-square-foot underground restaurant, cocktail bar, and karaoke lounge, which debuted on Wednesday, September 9 — diners enter by pressing a “rewind” button on an ’80s-style boombox that opens onto the bar. That’s where beverage director Ken Chen, formerly of Taipei’s Indulge Experimental Bistro, builds cocktails on tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Partner Alexander Lee’s menu includes truffle mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Beyond the restaurant are eight private karaoke rooms inspired by Hong Kong cinema, vintage recording studios, and other retro references. Rewind will also host a monthly guest bartender series featuring bartenders from New York spots like Stone & Soil, Yawning Cobra, and Red Sorghum. Rewind is co-founded by AYS Hospitality (behind NYC’s Mr. Moto’s collection of restaurants). 45-57 Davis Street, between Jackson and Skillman avenues

Lower East Side: Billed as “NYC’s most interesting sandwich shop,” ironically named Boring Sandwich opened inside a bodega on Saturday, September 5, with a globe-trotting assortment of gourmet sandwiches from chef Michael Brafman. The Shok-Shoe-Ka piles North African stewed tomato on an Aleppo bagel from Curly’s in Queens; a towering steak-and-egg Chivito pays homage to Uruguay’s national dish; and a New Orleans-styled muffuletta (a pressed Italian hero) also makes an appearance in the hidden dining destination that stays open until 10 p.m. Other orders include a tempura roll sandwich; chopped cheese riff; and another with Spam, tomato, crispy onion, and mala sauce. 97 Stanton Street, between Orchard and Ludlow streets

Soho: A new shop dedicated to single-source cacao with a bakery and cafe components, ÓOL, opened on Wednesday, September 9. Founder Ilana Gutierrez, who is from Mexico City, is showcasing single-origin cacao from Ecuador, Colombia, and Belize; it’s used for drinks with milks and/or water, along with spiced syrups like chile or ginger. ÓOL is partnering with NYC chain Breads Bakery for pastries made with that cacao, like a cacao swirl, cacao chop cookie, and a cacao croissant. In the near future, the two-story space will host tastings and workshops. 178 Spring Street, near Thomson Street

Tribeca: Keith McNally’s son, George, opened his first restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable. 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets

Tribeca: Evento, the nearly decade-old Italian hospitality company known for its cooking classes, culinary workshops, pasta-making dance parties, and big-ticket corporate events from Italian-born chef Andrea Belfiore and co-founder Sam Akiba, opened its first permanent home on Friday, September 4. The Manhattan flagship, housed inside the historic three-story Bogardus Mansion, is split up into three sections: a ground-floor cooking studio fit for pizza and pasta parties and workshops; a private dining room on the second floor dressed in Italian decor; and a forthcoming restaurant on the lower level. 75 Murray Street, between West Broadway and Greenwich Street

Upper East Side: Soba noodle house Kuriya, from the neighborhood team behind Japanese rice bowl restaurant Suki Desu, debuted on Sunday, September 6. Noodles presented on a tatami mat can be dipped in gyudon or topped with raw seafood, notes Infatuation. 219 E. 85th Street, between Second and Third avenues

Upper East Side: Bronx-born New York native, chef Lana Lagomarsini — a semifinalist on Top Chef season 22 and Gramercy Tavern alum — opens a supper clubby tasting menu spot centered on the Black culinary diaspora, on Wednesday, September 9. Creola, named after her grandmother, prepares courses like potlikker consomme (a nod to her grandmother’s collard greens) and oxtail pate en croute that riffs on the French pastry-wrapped meat dish. The $125 tasting menu is joined by $65 wine pairings. 1261 Park Avenue, between East 97th and 98th streets

Upper West Side: Derek Wu, the former manager of Lower East Side Chinese restaurant Wu’s Wonton King, heads across Central Park with the debut of Wu’s Dynasty on Thursday, September 3. As first reported by West Side Rag, the Cantonese newcomer is huge — it takes up 8,000 square feet — and does dim sum daily (with roving carts rolling around from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.). The parade of plates includes pan-fried Chinese chive and shrimp dumplings, pan-fried noodles with beef, cheong fun (steamed rice rolls), and custard lava buns. Live seafood and huge crustaceans like king crab greet customers upon entry inside tanks, and there’s Beijing duck, too. A bar serves cocktails, whiskeys, and wines. Hours run until 10 p.m. daily. 208 West 70th Street, between West End and Amsterdam avenues

Washington Heights: Eventually hoping to also be a bistro and bar, the ambitious new Boogie Lab opens as just an artisan bakery stocked with to-go loaves to start. “But this is just step one,” notes the team. Coming soon: food, drinks, music, and “an inviting space that shifts its rhythm from day to night.” 4015 Broadway, at West 169th Street

September 2

Spotlight

Midtown: After a revamp, iDen’s Beijing Duck House reopened on Tuesday, September 1, in its former La Grenouille space. The updated high-end duck restaurant originally opened in NYC last year, after its sibling location in Vancouver which had opened six years ago. The chef, Matt Chen, had run the kitchen of Le Palais in Taipei — apparently the first restaurant in Taiwan to receive three Michelin stars — retooled the menu, now featuring a $200 tasting menu as well as a la carte options like a duck-egg yolk roll; surf clam and okra salad; venison with Sichuan-pickled vegetables; and the Beijing duck, which starts at $128. 3 E. 52nd Street, between Fifth and Madison avenues

And the rest…

Chelsea: Showy clubstaurant STK Steakhouse has expanded its presence in the city, opening a spacious second location in Chelsea in mid-August. Diners — the space can fit 200 of them — will find the same steaks, seafood, cocktails, and “DJ-driven dining” (per a press release) that have kept the Midtown location going for nearly two decades. The restaurant will launch a seasonal pumpkin-focused menu beginning Wednesday, September 9, which includes offerings such as crab-stuffed shrimp in pumpkin cream sauce and pumpkin spice margaritas. The space was previously home to another flashy den of meat: Salt Bae’s Nusr-Et Steakhouse, which closed in 2024. 412 W. 15th Street, between Ninth and Tenth avenues

Chinatown: The team behind Essex Street’s old-timey photo booth Retrography unveiled a secret new cafe called Behind The Booth in the back on Wednesday, August 26. The slim-and-stylish setup specializes in an “unexpected” wine list and “ice cream you wouldn’t have ordered anywhere else,” per an opening message. 15 Essex Street, between Canal and Hester streets

Greenpoint: Acclaimed Lone Star pitmasters Jonny White and Chuck Charnichart brought Brooklyn a legit Texas barbecue joint on Sunday, August 30, with the opening of Kirbee’s. Their respective restaurants — Goldee’s in Fort Worth and Barbs B Q in Lockhart — are some of the best barbecue joints in the country over the last several years, with Michelin nods, James Beard nominations, and more. Charnichart’s barbecue plate features her South Texan and Mexican takes on barbecue: pork ribs with lime zest, brisket with Mexican spices, charro beans, and the iconic green spaghetti. White’s is more modern, with brisket, ribs, turkey, potato salad, and coleslaw. Each will include pickles and bread. Kirbee’s works like a true Texas barbecue: People line up outside the black-and-red storefront and place their orders at the first window; their orders will be cut up and plated inside; and then they’ll pick up their trays at the second window; after which they can either find a table in the 24-seat dining room. 55 McGuinness Boulevard South, between Engert Avenue and Newton Street

Greenpoint: Cozy corner coffee shop Loco Cafe opened in the small 500-square-foot space that was previously home to short-lived Viva La Pizza and Pizza Prince on Saturday, August 29, and the minimalist replacement inside has a winking cup of Joe logo. 626 Manhattan Avenue, at Nassau Avenue

Greenwich Village: The swanky martini destination Chateau Royale has been flipped into the more neighborhood-y Floradora, which opened on Thursday, August 27. The new menu features snacks such as mozzarella sticks and pigs in a blanket, alongside French dip sandwiches, burgers, disco fries, chicken paillard, two-layer oxtail lasagna, and more. (The drinks menu, meanwhile, leans into tiny ’tinis and other “sorta-’tinis.”) As owners Cody Pruitt and Jacob Cohen have told Eater NY, the flip was motivated by a desire to make the restaurant “more accessible, price-wise, as well as cuisine-wise, and vibe-wise, so we can see our neighbors more often;” diners at Chateau Royale tended to order the burger over the pricier Dover sole. It’s the second flip this summer for Pruitt and Cohen, who transitioned Libertine in the West Village into the “seafood tavern” Capitaine in June. 205 Thompson Street, at Bleecker Street

Upper East Side: Bright-orange Italian restaurant and pizzeria La Collina opened on Tuesday, August 18, for lunch, dinner, and brunch. Red and white pies join a namesake mozzarella salad and mains like Mediterranean sea bass with celery root puree or sirloin steak surrounded by roasted potatoes, plus a coconut Negroni or limoncello elixirs at the bar. A $34 two-course lunch option during the week features thinly sliced eggplant followed by tonnarelli cacio e pepe or tagliatelle Bolognese. 1431 First Avenue, at East 74th Street

West Village: NYC’s summer of Thai food continues on Wednesday, September 2, with the debut of Hommali from a trio of friends from Bangkok. The contemporary new spot rooted in Thailand’s beloved jasmine rice also offers a tom yum seafood cocktail; dry-aged duck breast served with fermented chile sauce; and penang curry with beef cheeks. A bar with a knack for fermentation and infusions slings drinks like the Tomato — a take on the michelada and a spritz, which includes a Singaporean rice wine made with jasmine and sticky rice. 28 Seventh Avenue South, near Leroy Street

Williamsburg: Small Change, a new bar from the team behind the Last Resort in the East Village and One Trick Pony in the West Village, opened in June in the former location of Lady Jay’s (which occupied the space for almost 15 years). The large backyard remains ready for group hangs, now with an awning of plants. Happy hour runs from 4 to 7 p.m., featuring draft beers and well drinks for $5, plus other drink specials. The beer-and-shot combo runs $8 all day. 633 Grand Street, near Leonard Street

Williamsburg: Finally, Ugly Baby has returned, having opened its new location on Thursday, August 27, in the corner spot that once housed Emmy Square Pizza. The restaurant first opened in Carroll Gardens in 2017 and quickly picked up a fervent following, who praised the restaurant’s intensely spicy dishes and its commitment to southern Thai dishes that were, at the time, less commonly found in the city. The popular and beloved restaurant closed in the final days of 2024, citing that chef Sirichai Sreparplarn was “tired and just needs a long break.” Sreparplarn is still behind the new version of Ugly Baby, which will have double the capacity of the original location and will feature a wider range of dishes. In Ugly Baby’s absence, some of its former employees went on to open Hungry Thirsty in the same location; it also welcomed a Manhattan sibling last month, the fiery Hungry Spicy. 364 Grand Street, between Havemeyer Street and Marcy Avenue

Update, 4:09 p.m.: This article, originally published at 10:55 a.m., has been updated to correctly reflect iDen’s Beijing Duck House’s reopening status.
